statement: To construct an icosahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures; and to prove that the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor.
heath_proof: Let the diameter AB of the given sphere be set out, and let it be cut at C so that AC is quadruple of CB, let the semicircle ADB be described on AB, let the straight line CD be drawn from C at right angles to AB, and let DB be joined; let the circle EFGHK be set out and let its radius be equal to DB, let the equilateral and equiangular pentagon EFGHK be inscribed in the circle EFGHK, let the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HK, KE be bisected at the points L, M, N, O, P, and let LM, MN, NO, OP, PL, EP be joined. Therefore the pentagon LMNOP is also equilateral, and the straight line EP belongs to a decagon. Now from the points E, F, G, H, K let the straight lines EQ, FR, GS, HT, KU be set up at right angles to the plane of the circle, and let them be equal to the radius of the circle EFGHK, let QR, RS, ST, TU, UQ, QL, LR, RM, MS, SN, NT, TO, OU, UP, PQ be joined. Now, since each of the straight lines EQ, KU is at right angles to the same plane, therefore EQ is parallel to KU. [XI. 6] But it is also equal to it; and the straight lines joining those extremities of equal and parallel straight lines which are in the same direction are equal and parallel. [I. 33] Therefore QU is equal and parallel to EK. But EK belongs to an equilateral pentagon; therefore QU also belongs to the equilateral pentagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK. For the same reason each of the straight lines QR, RS, ST, TU also belongs to the equilateral pentagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK; therefore the pentagon QRSTU is equilateral. And, since QE belongs to a hexagon, and EP to a decagon, and the angle QEP is right, therefore QP belongs to a pentagon; for the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the square on the side of the hexagon and the square on the side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle. [XIII. 10] For the same reason PU is also a side of a pentagon. But QU also belongs to a pentagon; therefore the triangle QPU is equilateral. For the same reason each of the triangles QLR, RMS, SNT, TOU is also equilateral. And, since each of the straight lines QL, QP was proved to belong to a pentagon, and LP also belongs to a pentagon, therefore the triangle QLP is equilateral. For the same reason each of the triangles LRM, MSN, NTO, OUP is also equilateral. Let the centre of the circle EFGHK the point V, be taken; from V let VZ be set up at right angles to the plane of the circle, let it be produced in the other direction, as VX, let there be cut off VW, the side of a hexagon, and each of the straight lines VX, WZ, being sides of a decagon, and let QZ, QW, UZ, EV, LV, LX, XM be joined. Now, since each of the straight lines VW, QE is at right angles to the plane of the circle, therefore VW is parallel to QE. [XI. 6] But they are also equal; therefore EV, QW are also equal and parallel. [I. 33] But EV belongs to a hexagon; therefore QW also belongs to a hexagon. And, since QW belongs to a hexagon, and WZ to a decagon, and the angle QWZ is right, therefore QZ belongs to a pentagon. [XIII. 10] For the same reason UZ also belongs to a pentagon, inasmuch as, if we join VK, WU, they will be equal and opposite, and VK, being a radius, belongs to a hexagon; [IV. 15] therefore WU also belongs to a hexagon. But WZ belongs to a decagon, and the angle UWZ is right; therefore UZ belongs to a pentagon. [XIII. 10] But QU also belongs to a pentagon; therefore the triangle QUZ is equilateral. For the same reason each of the remaining triangles of which the straight lines QR, RS, ST, TU are the bases, and the point Z the vertex, is also equilateral. Again, since VL belongs to a hexagon, and VX to a decagon, and the angle LVX is right, therefore LX belongs to a pentagon. [XIII. 10] For the same reason, if we join MV, which belongs to a hexagon, MX is also inferred to belong to a pentagon. But LM also belongs to a pentagon; therefore the triangle LMX is equilateral. Similarly it can be proved that each of the remaining triangles of which MN, NO, OP, PL are the bases, and the point X the vertex, is also equilateral. Therefore an icosahedron has been constructed which is contained by twenty equilateral triangles. It is next required to comprehend it in the given sphere, and to prove that the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor. For, since VW belongs to a hexagon, and WZ to a decagon, therefore VZ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, and VW is its greater segment; [XIII. 9] therefore, as ZV is to VW, so is VW to WZ. But VW is equal to VE, and WZ to VX; therefore, as ZV is to VE, so is EV to VX. And the angles ZVE, EVX are right; therefore, if we join the straight line EZ, the angle XEZ will be right because of the similarity of the triangles XEZ, VEZ. For the same reason, since, as ZV is to VW, so is VW to WZ, and ZV is equal to XW, and VW to WQ, therefore, as XW is to WQ, so is QW to WZ. And for this reason again, if we join QX, the angle at Q will be right; [VI. 8] therefore the semicircle described on XZ will also pass through Q. [III. 31] And if, XZ remaining fixed, the semicircle be carried round and restored to the same position from which it began to be moved, it will also pass through Q and the remaining angular points of the icosahedron, and the icosahedron will have been comprehended in a sphere. I say next that it is also comprehended in the given sphere. For let VW be bisected at A'. Then, since the straight line VZ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, and ZW is its lesser segment, therefore the square on ZW added to the half of the greater segment, that is WA', is five times the square on the half of the greater segment; [XIII. 3] therefore the square on ZA' is five times the square on. And ZX is double of ZA', and VW double of; therefore the square on ZX is five times the square on WV. And, since AC is quadruple of CB, therefore AB is five times BC. But, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BD; [VI. 8, V. Def. 9] therefore the square on AB is five times the square on BD. But the square on ZX was also proved to be five times the square on VW. And DB is equal to VW, for each of them is equal to the radius of the circle EFGHK; therefore AB is also equal to XZ. And AB is the diameter of the given sphere; therefore XZ is also equal to the diameter of the given sphere. Therefore the icosahedron has been comprehended in the given sphere I say next that the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor. For, since the diameter of the sphere is rational, and the square on it is five times the square on the radius of the circle EFGHK, therefore the radius of the circle EFGHK is also rational; hence its diameter is also rational. But, if an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle which has its diameter rational, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor. [XIII. 11] And the side of the pentagon EFGHK is the side of the icosahedron. Therefore the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor.
ai_proof_text:
13.16
**Statement:** To construct an icosahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures; and to prove that the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere, and let AB be taken as the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3), to which the irrationality of the side will be referred. From AB cut off a fifth part CB (6.9), so that AC is four times CB and AB is five times CB. Bisect AB (1.10), and with that midpoint as centre and half AB as distance describe the semicircle ADB on AB (P3, D1.18). At C draw CD at right angles to AB (1.11), meeting the semicircle at D, and join DB (P1).

**Step 2.** The angle ADB, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31). In the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DC has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB, so the triangle DBC is similar to the triangle ABD (6.8); hence the sides about the common angle at B are proportional, AB : BD = BD : BC (D6.1), and therefore the rectangle AB, BC is equal to the square on BD (6.17). Now AB is made up of five segments each equal to BC, so the rectangle AB, AB, that is the square on AB, is equal to five rectangles AB, BC (2.1). Therefore the square on AB is five times the square on BD.

**Step 3.** Take a point V, and with centre V and distance equal to DB describe the circle EFGHK (P3); VE, VF, VG, VH, VK are its radii, each equal to DB. In it inscribe the equilateral and equiangular pentagon EFGHK (4.11). Since the chords EF, FG, GH, HK, KE are equal, the arcs EF, FG, GH, HK, KE which they cut off are equal (3.28). Bisect these arcs at L, M, N, O, P respectively (3.30), and join LM, MN, NO, OP, PL and EL, LF, FM, MG, GN, NH, HO, OK, KP, PE (P1).

**Step 4.** The ten arcs EL, LF, FM, MG, GN, NH, HO, OK, KP, PE are halves of the five equal arcs, hence are all equal to one another; therefore the ten chords EL, LF, FM, MG, GN, NH, HO, OK, KP, PE are equal (3.29), so that ELFMGNHOKP is an equilateral decagon inscribed in the circle, and each of these chords is the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK. Further, the arc LM is made up of the arcs LF, FM, which are equal respectively to the arcs EL, LF making up the arc EF; hence the arc LM equals the arc EF, and the chord LM equals the chord EF (3.29). Similarly MN, NO, OP, PL each equal EF; thus LMNOP is an equilateral pentagon inscribed in the circle, with side equal to EF. Also the radius VE of the circle is equal to the side of the hexagon inscribed in it (4.15).

**Step 5.** Since the equilateral pentagon EFGHK is inscribed in the circle, the square on its side EF is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on the side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle (13.10); that is, the square on EF is equal to the squares on VE and EL together, where VE is the radius and EL is the side of the decagon.

**Step 6.** From the points E, F, G, H, K set up EQ, FR, GS, HT, KU at right angles to the plane of the circle EFGHK (11.12), all on the same side of the plane, and cut off each of them equal to the radius VE (1.3). Join QR, RS, ST, TU, UQ, and QL, LR, RM, MS, SN, NT, TO, OU, UP, PQ (P1).

**Step 7.** Since EQ and FR are at right angles to the same plane, they are parallel (11.6); and they are equal. Therefore QR, joining their extremities in the same directions, is equal and parallel to EF (1.33). Similarly RS = FG, ST = GH, TU = HK, UQ = KE. Hence each of QR, RS, ST, TU, UQ is equal to EF.

**Step 8.** Since EQ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, it makes right angles with EL, which lies in that plane and meets it (D11.3); so the angle QEL is right, and the square on QL is equal to the squares on QE and EL (1.47). But QE equals the radius VE, and EL is the side of the decagon; therefore the square on QL is equal to the square on EF (Step 5), and QL = EF. In the same way, since FL, FM, GM, GN, HN, HO, KO, KP, EP are each the side of the decagon, and FR, GS, HT, KU, EQ are each equal to the radius and at right angles to the plane, each of LR, RM, MS, SN, NT, TO, OU, UP, PQ is equal to EF.

**Step 9.** Therefore the ten triangles QLR, LRM, RMS, MSN, SNT, NTO, TOU, OUP, UPQ, PQL are equilateral, every side of each being equal to EF (Steps 4, 7, 8).

**Step 10.** From the centre V set up VZ at right angles to the plane of the circle (11.12), on the same side as EQ, and produce it through V to the other side of the plane (P2). On VZ cut off VW equal to the radius VE and WZ equal to EP, the side of the decagon, W lying between V and Z; and on the production cut off VX equal to EP (1.3). Join QZ, RZ, SZ, TZ, UZ, LX, MX, NX, OX, PX, and WQ, WR, WS, WT, WU (P1).

**Step 11.** Since VW and EQ are at right angles to the same plane, they are parallel (11.6); and they are equal, each being equal to VE. Therefore WQ, joining their extremities in the same directions, is equal and parallel to VE (1.33). Similarly WR = VF, WS = VG, WT = VH, WU = VK. Hence each of WQ, WR, WS, WT, WU is equal to the radius VE.

**Step 12.** Since VW is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle EVW is right (D11.3). Since WQ is parallel to VE and VW falls on them, the interior angles QWV, EVW on the same side are together equal to two right angles (1.29); hence the angle QWV is right. Then the angles QWV, QWZ, being adjacent angles on the straight line VZ, are together equal to two right angles (1.13); hence the angle QWZ is right. Therefore the square on QZ is equal to the squares on QW and WZ (1.47), that is, to the squares on the radius VE and on the side EP of the decagon, that is, to the square on EF (Step 5); so QZ = EF. Similarly RZ, SZ, TZ, UZ are each equal to EF. Therefore the five triangles QRZ, RSZ, STZ, TUZ, UQZ are equilateral, with every side equal to EF (Step 7).

**Step 13.** Since VZ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle ZVL is right (D11.3), and hence its adjacent angle XVL on the straight line ZX is also right (1.13). Therefore the square on LX is equal to the squares on LV and VX (1.47), that is, to the squares on the radius and on the side of the decagon, that is, to the square on EF (Step 5); so LX = EF. Similarly MX, NX, OX, PX are each equal to EF. Therefore the five triangles LMX, MNX, NOX, OPX, PLX are equilateral, with every side equal to EF (Step 4).

**Step 14.** Hence a solid figure has been constructed which is contained by the twenty triangles of Steps 9, 12 and 13, namely the ten triangles QLR, LRM, RMS, MSN, SNT, NTO, TOU, OUP, UPQ, PQL, the five triangles QRZ, RSZ, STZ, TUZ, UQZ, and the five triangles LMX, MNX, NOX, OPX, PLX. Each of these is equilateral and all their sides are equal to EF, so they are twenty equal and equilateral triangles; therefore the solid is an icosahedron (D11.27), and its side is equal to EF, the side of the pentagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK.

**Step 15.** Next, it is to be comprehended in a sphere. Since VW is the side of the hexagon and WZ the side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle EFGHK, and VZ is made up of them, VZ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, and VW is its greater segment (13.9). Bisect VW at Y (1.10). Then, VZ being cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, the square on the lesser segment ZW added to the half WY of the greater segment, that is, the square on ZY, is five times the square on WY (13.3).

**Step 16.** Since VW is bisected at Y, the square on VW is four times the square on WY (2.4). The angle QWY is right, being the angle QWV (Step 12). Therefore the square on QY is equal to the squares on QW and WY (1.47); and QW equals VE, which equals VW; so the square on QY is equal to four times the square on WY together with the square on WY, that is, to five times the square on WY, that is, to the square on ZY (Step 15). Hence QY = ZY. Similarly RY, SY, TY, UY are each equal to ZY.

**Step 17.** Since XV = WZ, each being equal to EP, and VY = YW, the whole XY is equal to the whole ZY (CN2). Again, since VZ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle LVY is right (D11.3); therefore the square on LY is equal to the squares on LV and VY (1.47). And LV is the radius, equal to VW, whose square is four times the square on VY (2.4); so the square on LY is five times the square on VY, that is, five times the square on WY, that is, the square on ZY (Step 15). Hence LY = ZY. Similarly MY, NY, OY, PY are each equal to ZY.

**Step 18.** Therefore the straight lines drawn from Y to all twelve vertices Q, R, S, T, U, L, M, N, O, P, X, Z are equal to YZ (Steps 16, 17). Describe on XZ the semicircle with centre Y and distance YZ (P3, D1.18), and let it be carried round about XZ, which remains fixed, until it is restored to the position from which it began to be moved; the figure so comprehended is a sphere (D11.14), of which XZ is a diameter and Y the centre (D11.17, D11.16). As the semicircle is carried round it passes through the plane containing XZ and any vertex, say Q; and in that plane, since YQ = YZ, the point Q lies on the circle with centre Y and distance YZ (D1.15), that is, on the surface of the sphere. The same holds for every vertex. Therefore the icosahedron has been comprehended in this sphere.

**Step 19.** This sphere is equal to the given sphere. For XZ is bisected at Y, so the square on XZ is four times the square on ZY (2.4), that is, four times five times the square on WY (Step 15), that is, five times four times the square on WY, that is, five times the square on VW (Step 16). But VW equals the radius VE, which equals DB; so the square on XZ is five times the square on DB, which is the square on AB (Step 2). Therefore XZ = AB, and the sphere on the diameter XZ is the given sphere. Thus the icosahedron has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 20.** Finally, the side of the icosahedron is minor. The diameter of the circle EFGHK is double the radius, that is, double DB, so its square is four times the square on DB (2.4). Since the square on AB is five times the square on DB (Step 2), five times the square on the diameter of the circle is twenty times the square on DB, which is four times the square on AB. Hence the square on the diameter of the circle has to the square on AB the ratio which the number 4 has to the number 5; therefore these squares are commensurable (10.6), so the diameter of the circle is commensurable in square with the rational straight line AB and is therefore itself rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 21.** Therefore the circle EFGHK has its diameter rational, and in it the equilateral pentagon EFGHK is inscribed; hence the side EF of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor (13.11). But every side of the icosahedron is equal to EF (Step 14). Therefore the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor. Q.E.F.
